docs.title: Distributed Inference Testbed
docs.text:
An experimental testbed for partitioned inference of deep neural networks and large language models across resource-constrained edge devices.

Five Raspberry Pi 4 boards on a dedicated IEEE 802.11ac wireless network, an edge server that hosts the access point, and a web application that drives every experiment end to end: scenario definition, concurrent Secure Shell (SSH) dispatch, layer-by-layer profiling under controlled compute and network conditions, measurement collection, and partition optimisation. Everything also runs on a single machine with no hardware at all.

The repository implements the testbed described in Chapter 3 ("Experimental Testbed Description") and Appendix B ("Testbed Implementation Details") of the PhD thesis Dynamic Partitioning and Resource Orchestration for AI Model Deployment in Resource-Constrained Wireless Edge Networks (Dimitrios Kafetzis, Athens University of Economics and Business, 2026). The thesis is the specification: every file, script and output name it cites is the name used here.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Complete experiment pipeline. One scenario file describes the model, the devices, the repetitions, the scheduling policy of the edge server, and per node the network conditions, the compute load and the hardware constraints. The pipeline applies it, profiles, collects, aggregates, optimises and tears everything down, in seven stages with a journal that undoes every change in reverse order, also on failure and after a restart.
  • Controlled conditions on real hardware. Traffic-control network emulation (tc-netem: delay with constant, uniform or square-wave variation, jitter, loss, rate cap, per destination), background traffic with iperf3, a duty-cycle compute load generator with the light, moderate and heavy regimes of the thesis, and hardware heterogeneity through cpufreq caps, cgroups v2 memory limits and thread counts.
  • Fine-grained measurement. Per-layer latency, memory and operation counts; per-phase timing of partitioned inference (local, transmission, queueing, remote); a 1 Hz resource monitor; INA260 power traces with energy and energy-delay product; ping latency and iperf3 throughput. All traces are aligned on an NTP-synchronised common origin.
  • Partition optimisation. The analytical delay model of the thesis for Round-Robin (RR) and Shortest-Job-First (SJF) scheduling at the edge server, with greedy, exhaustive and trend-based search, and a plug-in interface for new algorithms.
  • The NNPM web application. The Neural Network Architecture Partitioning (NNPM) manager: an interactive map of the topology with three-ping reachability probes every two seconds, click-to-add and draggable nodes, distance-derived link latencies, dialogs for scenario creation, benchmarking and optimisation, a live merged terminal, a results browser and a stop button that tears down cleanly.
  • Daemonless and reproducible. Nothing stays resident on a device beyond the SSH server: every device-side process is started for the duration of an experiment and stopped at its end. Scenarios are versioned and replayable, random seeds are set on every node, dependencies are hash-pinned per role and platform, and provisioning installs from a versioned local package mirror with a verifiable manifest.
  • Runs without hardware. A local mode simulates every node on one machine with a fake model, dry-run shaping and a fake /sys tree. The whole pipeline, the web application and the provisioning scripts are exercised this way in continuous integration.
  • Extensible. Any tf.keras.applications classifier and any Hugging Face decoder of a known family (GPT-2, Llama, Mistral, Qwen2, Gemma) run through generic adapters with automatic cut points; model parameters, input sources (files, image folders with labels, prompts) and a partition-equivalence check are scenario fields; a model catalogue with checksums holds the weights. See docs/adding_a_model.md.
  • Runtime plug-ins. An inference runtime is a plug-in with a scenario block, readiness checks, maintenance actions and a results parser, all driven from NNPM. The author's HeadSplit runtime for head-level partitioning of decoder-only LLMs is the first: installed from the mirror at a pinned commit, prepared (profile, checkpoint) and run from the web application under the testbed's shaping, load, monitors and metadata. See docs/adding_a_runtime.md.

    SRV["Partitioned-inference service (RR, SJF)<br/>src/inference/server.py"]
    AP[("Access point, DHCP and DNS,<br/>NTP server, package mirror")]
  end
  subgraph DEV["Edge device i (Raspberry Pi 4, Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit)"]
    PROF["Profiler and inference client<br/>src/models/, src/inference/client.py"]
    MON["Resource, power and latency monitors<br/>src/testbed/, src/network/"]
    CTRL["Load generator, tc-netem, cpufreq, cgroups<br/>src/testbed/"]
  end
  NNPM --> ORCH --> SSH
  SSH -- "management network (Ethernet)" --> PROF
  SSH -- "management network (Ethernet)" --> MON
  SSH -- "management network (Ethernet)" --> CTRL
  PROF -- "data plane (IEEE 802.11ac)" --> SRV
  PROF -. "result files" .-> AGG
  MON -. "traces" .-> AGG

The testbed has three layers. The NNPM manager (web application and orchestration package) runs each experiment from start to finish. The measurement infrastructure runs on the devices only while an experiment is in progress: profiler, inference client, resource and power monitors, latency and throughput tools. The system runtime is the operating system and the frameworks installed by provisioning from a local mirror. Management traffic (SSH, result collection, NTP, packages) uses a wired network; inference traffic, latency measurement and shaping use the wireless data plane, so the two never interfere. The full description, stage by stage, is in docs/architecture.md.

docs.title: On the hardware
docs.text:
1. Assemble the testbed as in the setup guide: five Raspberry Pi 4 boards on an open rack, an edge server with a USB IEEE 802.11ac adapter for the isolated access point, and an Ethernet switch for the management network. The bill of materials is in the guide.
  2. Edge server. Copy config.example.yaml to config.yaml and nodes.example.json to nodes.json, edit them, then run scripts/provision/provision_edge_server.sh --allow-upstream followed by scripts/provision/build_mirror.sh wheels. This configures the access point, DHCP and DNS, the NTP server, the package mirror and the NNPM service.
  3. Devices. Flash Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm 64-bit, run scripts/provision/prepare_image.sh <node id> <boot partition>, boot the board on the switch, then run scripts/provision/provision_device.sh <node id> (after build_mirror.sh apt <node id> once). Every device is installed from the mirror only.
  4. Check. Open http://<edge server management address>:8001/; every marker should be green within a few seconds. Run scripts/base_station/run_full_benchmarking.sh examples/scenarios/baseline.yaml and find the three output files in results/latest/.
  5. Validate. Work through the hardware validation checklist: the physical checks that the test suite cannot perform, each with its expected outcome.

Every provisioning script accepts --dry-run and prints the commands it would run.

docs.title: Running experiments
docs.text:
A scenario is one YAML or JSON object. The example below profiles AlexNet on four devices under different compute loads, runs partitioned inference at five partition points, and sweeps the scheduling policy of the edge server:

name: ch4_validation
model: alexnet
devices: [device1, device2, device3, device4]
repetitions: 5
seed: 2024
edge_server: {policy: SJF, nominal_frequency: true, profile_capacity: true}
inference: {enabled: true, partition_points: [0, 2, 4, 8, 11], repetitions: 50}
load:
  device2: {mode: processes, processes: 1}
  device3: {mode: processes, processes: 2}
  device4: {mode: processes, processes: 3}
optimisation: {enabled: true, algorithm: greedy, objective: total_delay}
sweep: {path: edge_server.policy, values: [RR, SJF]}

Run it from NNPM (Create scenario, then Save and run) or from the command line:

scripts/base_station/run_experiment.sh examples/scenarios/ch4_validation.yaml
scripts/base_station/run_full_benchmarking.sh examples/scenarios/baseline.yaml   # profiling only, no load or shaping
scripts/base_station/clean_devices.sh                                            # undo a run interrupted by a crash
cd results/latest && ../../.venv/bin/python -m src.partitioning.delay_optimizer \
    calculated_max_partition_points.json total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json \
    final_latencies_averages.json --scheduling_algorithm SJF --mode optimize     # optimise a finished run again

Every run writes one directory under results/, with the scenario version, the run metadata (software versions, hardware facts and NTP status of every node, recorded before any change), the journal, the merged log, the raw records and traces, and the three aggregated outputs the thesis names: total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json, calculated_max_partition_points.json and final_latencies_averages.json. The scenario reference lists every field with its default; the results format describes every file. Example scenarios for the Chapter 4 validation and the Chapter 6 heterogeneity and round-trip-time studies are in examples/scenarios/.

docs.title: Provenance and related work
docs.text: This repository continues the author's earlier DNN-Partitioning-and-Offloading-Testbed, first presented as a demonstration at ACM MobiHoc 2024. The code was rewritten so that it implements the testbed exactly as the thesis describes it; the earlier repository remains available as reference material. HeadSplit, the author's runtime for head-level LLM partitioning with inter-layer speculation (Chapter 6), is integrated as an optional external component.

docs.title: Adding a model
docs.text:
A model is an adapter: a sequence of S stages with, per stage, its operation count and the size of its output, plus the means to run stages 1..s and s+1..S separately. Partition point s means that stages 1..s run on the device and s+1..S on the edge server (s = 0 sends the raw input, s = S runs everything locally). Everything else in the testbed, the profiler, the partitioned-inference service and client, the aggregation and the optimiser, works on that interface (src/models/registry.py, ModelAdapter).

Three ways to add a model, from cheapest to most general:

docs.title: 1. A name and a parameter
docs.text:
Many models need no code at all:

  • Any tf.keras.applications classifier: model: keras_app with model_args: {application: InceptionV3}; or one of the registered names mobilenetv2, efficientnetb0, densenet121, resnet50v2, inceptionv3, nasnetmobile, xception. The adapter (src/models/tf/keras_applications.py) finds the cut points automatically: the layers whose output is the only tensor crossing from the layers before them to the layers after them, thinned to max_stages boundaries at roughly equal shares of the multiply-accumulate operations. num_classes and input_size are parameters.
  • Any Hugging Face decoder-only model whose family is in the family table (GPT-2, Llama, Mistral, Qwen2, Gemma): model: hf_decoder with model_args: {checkpoint: <directory on the device or model name in its cache>, seq_len: 64}, or without a checkpoint model_args: {config: {model_type: llama, num_hidden_layers: 4, ...}} for random weights. llama32_1b and qwen25_05b are registered with their published configurations, like gpt2 and tinyllama.

Model parameters are listed in the catalogue (GET /api/catalog, model_parameters) and rendered by the Create scenario dialog under the model drop-down. They are validated against the adapter's PARAMETERS schema when a run starts and passed to every device tool as --model-args.

docs.title: 2. A subclass of a base adapter
docs.text:
When the model is a sequence of Keras layer groups, subclass SequentialStageAdapter (src/models/tf/keras_stages.py) and return the stages:

"""MyNet: four stages."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

import tensorflow as tf

from src.models.registry import register
from src.models.tf.keras_stages import SequentialStageAdapter

L = tf.keras.layers


class MyNetAdapter(SequentialStageAdapter):
    name = "mynet"
    input_shape: tuple[int, ...] = (64, 64, 3)
    PARAMETERS = {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"num_classes": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 2, "default": 10}},
    }

    def __init__(self, num_classes: int = 10) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.num_classes = num_classes

    def define_stages(self) -> list[tuple[str, list[Any]]]:
        return [
            ("conv1", [L.Conv2D(16, 3, activation="relu", name="conv1")]),
            ("pool1", [L.MaxPooling2D(2, name="pool1")]),
            ("conv2", [L.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu", name="conv2")]),
            ("fc", [L.Flatten(), L.Dense(self.num_classes, activation="softmax", name="fc")]),
        ]


ADAPTERS = {"mynet": MyNetAdapter}
register("mynet", MyNetAdapter)

The base class traces the model once to record shapes and operation counts (src/models/flops.py knows convolutions, depthwise and separable convolutions, dense and recurrent layers, pooling, normalisation and the element-wise layers), stores weights as .npz, and implements run_stages.

  • A functional graph with skip connections: subclass FunctionalCutAdapter, return the model from define_model() and name the cut layers in cuts (ResNet-50 does this), or override select_cuts(model) to compute them (keras_applications.py does this).
  • A decoder-only PyTorch model of a known family: subclass DecoderStageAdapter (src/models/torch/decoder.py), set family and return the Hugging Face configuration from hf_config() (gpt2.py, tinyllama.py, hf_decoder.py). A new family is one more row of FAMILIES: attribute paths of the layers, the attention and feed-forward modules, the norms and the embeddings, and a few structural flags (fused projections, rotary positions, gated feed-forward block, scaled embeddings). The head-wise decomposition and the hook profiler follow the table.

docs.title: 3. An adapter from scratch
docs.text: Implement the protocol directly when the model is neither (src/models/fake.py is the smallest complete example): name, framework, input_shape, stages, input_bytes, build(seed), load_weights, save_weights, make_input(seed), run_stages(x, start, stop), serialize, deserialize. run_stages must be exact: stages 1..s then s+1..S must equal 1..S on the same input (float tolerance), which is what the profiler and the partitioned-inference measurements assume and what python -m src.models.inference verify checks.

docs.title: Where to put it and how it reaches the devices
docs.text:
• Inside the repository: a module under src/models/tf/ or src/models/torch/ listed in BUILTIN_MODULES of src/models/registry.py. The repository is synchronised to every device at provisioning, so the adapter is available there.
  • Outside the repository: a module importable on the edge server and on the devices, named in TESTBED_MODEL_MODULES (comma-separated), or an installed package with a testbed.models entry point. The devices need the module too: the simplest way is a directory synchronised with the code.

docs.title: Weights and inputs
docs.text:
• Random weights with the scenario's seed are the default (train_and_run_benchmark.sh train prepares them on the device). Real weights go through the model catalogue (<bs_models_dir>/models.yaml, example in examples/models.yaml; python -m src.models.weights fetch NAME --allow-upstream obtains them, verify checks the checksums, build_mirror.sh models puts them in the mirror). Provisioning copies bs_models_dir to the devices; NNPM's Runtimes dialog distributes a checkpoint on demand.
  • Inputs: the scenario's input block (synthetic, numpy_file, image_file, image_folder, text_prompt); see scenario_reference.md. Image sources resize to the model's input; an image folder with class sub-directories gives a label, so verify reports top-1 accuracy as well.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Every adapter has a test that builds a small configuration (no download), asserts the stage shapes and the partition equivalence at every cut, and round-trips the weights (tests/test_tf_models.py, tests/test_torch_models.py). Mark tests that build real models slow; the fast suite must not import TensorFlow or PyTorch.

docs.title: Adding a runtime
docs.text:
A runtime is what the profile stage of an experiment runs. The built-in testbed runtime profiles the model layer by layer on every device and runs partitioned inference against the edge-server service. An external runtime runs its own distributed inference on the devices (HeadSplit is the first), under the testbed's scenario: shaping, load, heterogeneity, monitors, power traces, metadata, journal and teardown. Aggregation and optimisation are skipped for external runtimes, since they produce no per-layer profile.

The interface (src/orchestration/runtimes/__init__.py, Runtime) is what NNPM needs to configure and manage a runtime without knowing it:

Member Purpose name, label, description, external the catalogue entry and the runtime selector of the Create scenario dialog schema JSON Schema of the scenario block scenario[name]; the dialog renders it (x-nnpm: {widget: node} gives a device drop-down, nodes device check boxes, hidden skips a field); the block joins the scenario schema, so validate() accepts it run(ctx) the profile stage: start device processes with ctx.start_device_process (tagged, journaled, stopped at teardown), run commands with ctx.executor, write results under ctx.paths.root, put the main figures in ctx.outputs check_node(session, node, params) readiness checks of one device, as Check(name, status, detail) rows (ok, warn, fail, skip); the Runtimes dialog shows them as a table actions() and perform(action, params, session) maintenance actions (install, build a profile, distribute a checkpoint) with their parameter schemas; they run as tasks, one at a time, never during an experiment, logging to the terminal results(run_dir) the parsed results of a finished run for the run summary page

ActionSession gives checks and actions the live transport (session.executor, SSH or local processes), a command runner for the edge server (session.run_local, injectable in tests), session.copy_to_node (rsync, or a plain copy in local mode), the configuration, the topology, a log sink and a cancel flag.

docs.title: A minimal runtime
docs.text:
"""Echo runtime: runs one command per device and records its output."""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from src.common.nodes import Node
from src.common.runs import write_json_atomic
from src.orchestration.runtimes import ActionSession, ActionSpec, Check


class EchoRuntime:
    name = "echo"
    label = "Echo (example)"
    description = "Runs `hostname` on every device and stores the answers."
    external = True

    @property
    def schema(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {"type": "object", "properties": {"greeting": {"type": "string", "default": "hi"}}}

    def run(self, ctx: Any) -> None:
        settings = ctx.scenario.get("echo", {})
        outcomes = ctx.executor.run_on_nodes(ctx.devices, f"echo {settings['greeting']}; hostname")
        answers = {node_id: o.stdout.strip() for node_id, o in outcomes.items()}
        write_json_atomic(ctx.paths.root / "echo" / "results.json", answers)
        ctx.outputs["echo"] = answers

    def check_node(self, session: ActionSession, node: Node, params: dict[str, Any]) -> list[Check]:
        outcome = session.executor.run_on_node(node, "command -v hostname", check=False)
        return [Check("hostname", "ok" if outcome.ok else "fail", outcome.stdout.strip())]

    def actions(self) -> list[ActionSpec]:
        return []

    def perform(self, action: str, params: dict[str, Any], session: ActionSession) -> None:
        raise KeyError(action)

    def results(self, run_dir: Path) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
        path = run_dir / "echo" / "results.json"
        return {"kind": "echo", "answers": path.read_text()} if path.exists() else None


RUNTIME = EchoRuntime()

Register it: a module in TESTBED_RUNTIME_MODULES (comma-separated), a testbed.runtimes entry point, or, inside the repository, a module under src/orchestration/runtimes/ listed in BUILTIN_MODULES. A scenario then says runtime: echo and carries an echo block; NNPM lists the runtime in the Create scenario dialog and in the Runtimes dialog.

docs.title: Rules every runtime follows
docs.text:
• Daemonless. Device-side processes are started through ctx.start_device_process (a tagged detached process, recorded in the journal) or run to completion through the executor. Teardown stops what the journal lists and anything with the run's tag.
  • Undo at teardown. A runtime applies no device setting of its own; the scenario's shaping, load and heterogeneity are applied and undone by the pipeline. If a runtime must change something, it records an undo entry with ctx.record and handles it in undo_entry of src/orchestration/experiment.py.
  • Testable without hardware. Checks and actions are exercised against FakeTransport and FakeRunner (every command string asserted) and in local mode against stub scripts (tests/test_runtimes.py, tests/integration/test_headsplit_runtime.py).
  • Results in the run directory. Under results/<run id>/<runtime name>/, with the main figures in ctx.outputs so that the Runs panel, the summary page and the sweep table can show them.

HeadSplit (src/orchestration/runtimes/headsplit.py) is the reference implementation; headsplit_integration.md describes what it does.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This document describes how the testbed software is organised and how an experiment flows through it. It follows Chapter 3 ("Experimental Testbed Description") and Appendix B of the thesis; where a name appears in the thesis (a file, a script, an output file), the code uses the same name.

docs.title: Three layers
docs.text:
1. The Neural Network Architecture Partitioning (NNPM) manager runs each experiment from start to finish: scenario configuration, concurrent Secure Shell (SSH) execution across the devices, profiling, collection and partition optimisation. It is a web application served from the edge server (gui/) on top of the orchestration package (src/orchestration/), which the command-line scripts in scripts/base_station/ use as well.
  2. The measurement infrastructure runs on the devices for the duration of an experiment: the per-layer profiler (src/models/profiler.py), the per-phase timing client of partitioned inference (src/inference/client.py), the resource-monitoring agent (src/testbed/resource_monitor.py), the power monitor (src/network/power_measurement.py), the latency and throughput measurements (src/network/), and, on the edge server, the aggregation pipeline (src/benchmarking/) that produces the inputs of the analytical models.
  3. The system runtime is pre-existing software installed on every node: Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) with Python 3.11, TensorFlow and PyTorch on the devices; Ubuntu with the same Python and frameworks on the edge server. Provisioning (scripts/provision/) installs and configures it from a local package mirror.
flowchart LR
  subgraph Edge server
    NNPM[NNPM web application<br/>gui/]
    ORCH[Orchestration<br/>src/orchestration/]
    SSH[SSH dispatch<br/>src/network/ssh_executor.py]
    AGG[Aggregation and optimisation<br/>src/benchmarking/, src/partitioning/]
    SRV[Inference service RR/SJF<br/>src/inference/server.py]
    AP[(Access point, DHCP/DNS, NTP, mirror)]
  end
  subgraph Device i
    PROF[Profiler and inference client<br/>src/models/, src/inference/client.py]
    MON[Monitor, power, latency<br/>src/testbed/, src/network/]
    LOAD[Load generator, tc-netem, cpufreq, cgroups<br/>src/testbed/]
  end
  NNPM --> ORCH --> SSH
  SSH -- management network --> PROF
  SSH -- management network --> MON
  SSH -- management network --> LOAD
  PROF -- data plane --> SRV
  PROF -. result files .-> AGG
  MON -. traces .-> AGG

The edge server talks to the devices over the wired management network (SSH, result collection, NTP, package mirror); the devices talk to the edge server's inference service over the wireless data plane, which is also where latency is measured and shaping is applied. nodes.json holds both addresses of every node; src/common/nodes.py chooses the right one for each subsystem.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Path Content config.example.yaml, nodes.example.json the two configuration files, copied to config.yaml and nodes.json at the repository root (src/config.py, src/common/nodes.py) src/common/ infrastructure used everywhere: command runners (real, fake, dry run), clocks, rooted /sys access, tagged detached processes, run directories and the run journal, seeds, the coordinated start signal, run metadata, the device probe src/network/ the transport and SSH dispatch layer, result collection, latency, throughput and power measurement, node statistics src/testbed/ device-side control: load generator, tc-netem shaping, background traffic, heterogeneity (cpufreq, cgroups, threads), resource monitor, edge-server frequency policy src/models/ model adapters (TensorFlow: AlexNet, VGG-16, ResNet-50, GRU predictor, any tf.keras.applications classifier with automatic cuts; PyTorch: GPT-2, TinyLlama, Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5 0.5B, any Hugging Face decoder of a known family; a fake model), analytical operation counts, the profiler, the device-side inference entry point with the partition check, input sources, the model catalogue, head-wise LLM decomposition and hook-based profiling src/inference/ the partitioned-inference service of the edge server (RR and SJF scheduling), its wire protocol and the device client with per-phase timing src/benchmarking/ measurement records and their schema, aggregation over repetitions and trace merging, partition feasibility src/partitioning/ the Chapter 4 delay model, the search algorithms (greedy, exhaustive, trend-based) and delay_optimizer.py src/orchestration/ scenarios (schema, versions, sweeps), the experiment pipeline, local mode, the map rule, the runtime plug-ins (runtimes/: the testbed runtime and HeadSplit) src/provisioning/ template rendering and the mirror manifest used by the provisioning scripts gui/ the NNPM web application: Flask blueprints, the page, vendored Leaflet scripts/base_station/ run_full_benchmarking.sh, run_experiment.sh, clean_devices.sh scripts/end_device/ train_and_run_benchmark.sh, transfer_files.sh, apply_latency.sh scripts/provision/ provisioning scripts and templates docs/ this documentation and the JSON Schemas examples/scenarios/ example scenarios, including the Chapter 4 and Chapter 6 procedures data/sample/ synthetic sample output files (labelled as such) requirements/ direct dependencies and hash-pinned lock files per role tests/ pytest suite, including the local-mode integration tests and golden files

docs.title: An experiment, stage by stage
docs.text:
A scenario (one JSON object, validated against docs/schemas/scenario.schema.json) names the model, the devices, the repetitions and seed, the edge-server policy, and, per node, the network conditions, the compute load and the heterogeneity settings. src/orchestration/experiment.py runs it in seven stages; every change a stage makes on a node is recorded in the run journal before the next step, so that the last stage can undo it.

Stage What happens Where preflight the run directory is created; metadata.json records the scenario, the Git commit, the framework versions, the kernel version and the NTP status of every node, before any change; a node whose NTP offset exceeds ntp_offset_threshold_ms stops the run src/common/metadata.py, src/common/probe.py apply edge-server frequency policy; per-node cpufreq cap, memory cgroup and thread count; tc-netem shaping (constant, uniform or square-wave delay, jitter, loss, rate cap); background traffic; load generators; monitoring agents and power monitors; then a settling time src/testbed/ profile a start instant T0 is chosen and passed to every device; each device waits for it, captures its time origin and profiles the model layer by layer (train_and_run_benchmark.sh); the edge server profiles its own capacity; optionally the devices run partitioned inference against the edge-server service and record the local, transmission and remote phases; with checks.partition_equivalence every device compares the partition points with the unpartitioned model; the stage belongs to the scenario's runtime, and an external runtime (runtime: headsplit) runs its own controller and workers instead src/models/, src/inference/, src/orchestration/runtimes/ collect latency and system-metric capture on every device; the edge server copies the result files over SSH and prefixes each name with the device hostname src/network/latency_measurement.py, src/network/collection.py aggregate final_latencies_averages.json (node statistics, also written into nodes.json), total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json (per-device averages over repetitions and the merged traces), calculated_max_partition_points.json (feasibility) src/network/node_statistics.py, src/benchmarking/ optimise the partition vector for the scenario's objective under the chosen scheduling policy, written next to the scenario version with the hashes of its inputs src/partitioning/delay_optimizer.py teardown the journal entries are undone in reverse order (stop processes, clear shaping, restore frequencies, remove cgroups), then every remaining tagged process on each device is stopped; this runs on success, on failure and, through teardown or clean_devices.sh, after a restart src/common/runs.py, src/orchestration/experiment.py

The benchmarking pipeline (run_full_benchmarking.sh, the Benchmarking dialog) is the four-stage subset of Appendix B: dispatch, collection, post-processing and outputs; it applies no load and no shaping.

docs.title: Daemonless operation
docs.text: Nothing of the testbed stays resident on a device. Each device-side process (monitor, load generator, latency injector, power monitor, inference client, HeadSplit worker) is started over SSH as a detached process in its own session and process group, carries a tag testbed-<run id>-<component> in its environment and as a --tag argument, and has its process-group id written to a PID file. Stopping a component kills its process group; clean_devices.sh finds survivors by tag. The only requirement on a device is the operating system with its SSH server and the inference runtime (src/common/process_tags.py).

docs.title: Measurement conventions
docs.text: Intervals are integers in nanoseconds from time.perf_counter_ns(). Every record carries an origin, the NTP-synchronised wall clock and the monotonic counter captured together at the start signal, so traces from different devices can be aligned during aggregation. Memory is in mebibytes, CPU in percent, sizes in bytes. The record formats are described in results_format.md.

docs.title: Local mode
docs.text: Every component can run without hardware. In local mode (--local), each node becomes a working directory under one root; device-side commands run as local subprocesses, the privileged tools (tc, cpufreq, cgroups) run in dry-run mode or against a fake /sys tree, the inference service listens on the loopback interface and the fake model stands in for a real network. The continuous-integration workflow runs the whole pipeline this way, and NNPM can be demonstrated on a laptop with nnpm --local.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project are documented in this file. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and the project uses Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• An NNPM tutorial (docs/nnpm_tutorial.md) with screenshots of every view, taken in local mode by scripts/docs/nnpm_screenshots.py (Playwright).
  • A documentation website built with MkDocs (Material) from docs/ (mkdocs.yml, requirements/docs.lock), published to GitHub Pages on every push and built strictly in CI.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The runtime drop-down of the Create scenario dialog listed HeadSplit first and selected it by default; testbed is now first and selected.
  • Form fields rendered from a schema appeared in alphabetical order because Flask 3 sorts JSON keys; the schema's order is kept.
  • The run summary page printed the scenario version as a raw mapping.
  • Documentation: the edge server is an Intel Core i7-5820K (setup guide); the version tables name the thesis software table as the list of pinned versions; the hardware checklist expects Transformers 4.46.3; the collection and aggregation docstrings describe the pull collection and the per-record time origins.

Extensions beyond the thesis: runtime plug-ins with HeadSplit managed from NNPM, generic model adapters, a model catalogue, input sources and a partition check. The thesis requirements keep their status; the hardware checklist gains a section for these extensions.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Runtime plug-ins (src/orchestration/runtimes/): an inference runtime exposes its scenario block as a JSON Schema, per-device readiness checks, maintenance actions and a results parser; runtimes register like models and algorithms. The built-in testbed runtime and HeadSplit are the two implementations; docs/adding_a_runtime.md explains the interface.
  • HeadSplit through NNPM: the Create scenario dialog has a runtime selector and renders the HeadSplit block (controller, workers, model, tokens, mode, speculation parameters); the Runtimes dialog checks every device (checkout and commit, environment, profile, checkpoint) and offers three actions (install or update from the mirror, build the speculation profile on the edge server and copy it to the controller, distribute a checkpoint with checksum verification), run as tasks that log to the terminal; the run summary page shows the per-mode results. A controller that accepts --json (HeadSplit v0.1.0 and later) is used in preference to the summary lines.
  • Sweeps from NNPM: a field path and values in the Create scenario dialog; the variants run one after the other, each carrying sweep_origin; the run summary page (/runs/<id>) groups them with their main figures.
  • Model parameters (model_args): adapters declare a PARAMETERS schema (classes, sequence length, configuration overrides, application, checkpoint); scenarios pass the values, validated when the run starts, to every device tool; the dialog renders the fields of the chosen model.
  • Generic adapters: any tf.keras.applications classifier with automatic single-tensor cut points thinned to stages of comparable work (MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and others by name); any Hugging Face decoder through a family table (GPT-2, Llama, Mistral, Qwen2, Gemma), with Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen2.5 0.5B registered. docs/adding_a_model.md explains the three ways to add a model.
  • Model catalogue (bs_models_dir/models.yaml, python -m src.models.weights list|verify|checksums|fetch, build_mirror.sh models): seeded weights, Keras ImageNet weights and Hugging Face checkpoints with SHA256SUMS.
  • Input sources (input block: synthetic, numpy_file, image_file, image_folder with class labels, text_prompt) recorded in every measurement, and the partition-equivalence check (checks.partition_equivalence, python -m src.models.inference verify: deviation per partition point, top-1 agreement, accuracy with a label).
  • Project documentation for contributors: CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md, this changelog, issue and pull-request templates.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thank you for your interest in the Distributed Inference Testbed. This document explains how to set up a development environment, which checks a change must pass, and the conventions the code base follows.

docs.title: Development set-up
docs.text:
Any Linux machine with Python 3.11; no testbed hardware is needed.

git clone https://github.com/Dimitrios-Kafetzis/Distributed-Inference-Testbed.git
cd Distributed-Inference-Testbed
uv venv .venv --python 3.11
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --require-hashes -r requirements/dev.lock

requirements/dev.lock contains the edge-server stack plus pytest, ruff, mypy and shellcheck. The real TensorFlow and PyTorch models (the slow tests) need requirements/edge_server.lock as well; see docs/installation.md.

docs.title: Checks that must pass
docs.text:
Run these before opening a pull request. The continuous-integration workflow runs the same commands.

.venv/bin/ruff check . && .venv/bin/ruff format --check .
.venv/bin/mypy
.venv/bin/shellcheck -x $(git ls-files '*.sh')
.venv/bin/pytest -m "not slow"
.venv/bin/pytest -m slow            # when a change touches the model adapters or the profiler

The documentation site is built with MkDocs from docs/ (mkdocs.yml; requirements/docs.lock holds the tooling): uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --require-hashes -r requirements/docs.lock && .venv/bin/mkdocs serve previews it, and mkdocs build --strict must pass (it runs in CI). The NNPM screenshots of the tutorial are regenerated with python scripts/docs/nnpm_screenshots.py --server-python .venv/bin/python (Playwright, from the same lock, after python -m playwright install chromium).

A change to the provisioning scripts or templates usually changes the dry-run command plans; regenerate the golden files with UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 .venv/bin/pytest tests/test_provisioning.py and review the diff before committing it.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• The thesis is the specification. File, script and output names cited in the thesis (for example src/config.py, gui/app.py, run_full_benchmarking.sh, total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json) must keep their names; tests/test_thesis_names.py enforces this. The software role string of the edge server is Base Station.
  • Everything runs without hardware. Every external effect (commands, SSH, /sys, clocks, sensors) goes through an injectable runner, transport, clock or rooted file system, so that it can be faked or dry-run in tests. A new device-side tool needs a --dry-run path and a unit test with a fake runner.
  • Daemonless. Nothing of the testbed stays resident on a device. A process that runs on a device is started over SSH as a tagged detached process for the duration of an experiment and stopped at its end (src/common/process_tags.py).
  • Undo everything. A change made on a device during a run (shaping, frequency, cgroup, load, process) is recorded in the run journal before the next step, with its undo action, so that teardown can revert it, also on failure.
  • Small modules, strict types. Python 3.11, mypy --strict, ruff with a line length of 100. Prefer plain functions and dataclasses; keep a module to one responsibility.
  • Pinned dependencies. Direct dependencies live in requirements/*.in; the lock files are regenerated with scripts/lock_requirements.sh and the mirror rebuilt afterwards. Do not edit a lock file by hand.
  • No secrets, no personal data. Secrets come only from environment variables named in config.yaml. Addresses and home directories do not appear in code (tests/test_no_hardcoded_literals.py). Sample data shipped in the repository is synthetic and labelled as such.
  • Documentation and comments are in British English, in plain wording, and are updated in the same change as the code. Every relative link must resolve (tests/test_docs_links.py). Give the full name first, then the acronym in parentheses.

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• One logical change per commit, with a short imperative subject line that states what the change does.
  • A pull request describes the motivation, the change, how it was tested, and whether it was verified on the physical testbed. Changes that can only be verified on the hardware should say so and name the item of docs/hardware_validation_checklist.md that covers them.
  • Keep the change focused; refactoring that is not needed for the change belongs in a separate pull request.

docs.title: Reporting problems
docs.text: Use the issue templates: a bug report should include the scenario, the run's metadata.json and summary.json where applicable, and the relevant part of logs/merged.log. Please remove addresses and host names you do not want to publish.

docs.title: Hardware validation checklist
docs.text: Everything in this repository is tested without hardware: with fake command runners, fake clocks, a fake sysfs tree and a local mode that simulates all nodes on one machine. The items below are the physical checks that only the real testbed can answer. Each item names the requirement it closes (IDs from the thesis requirement catalogue), the steps, and the expected outcome. Record the outcome and the date next to each item.

docs.title: Software stack (A-07, J-19)
docs.text:
• [ ] On one Raspberry Pi 4 (Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm 64-bit, Python 3.11): create a virtual environment and install requirements/edge_device.lock with pip install --require-hashes -r requirements/edge_device.lock. Expected: every wheel is found for aarch64 and cp311; python -c "import tensorflow; print(tensorflow.__version__)" prints 2.15.1.
  • [ ] Same device: install requirements/edge_device_llm.lock. Expected: torch 2.1.2 and transformers 4.46.3 import; torch.get_num_threads() returns 4.
  • [ ] Note the wall-clock time of each installation (J-15; the thesis states about 25 minutes per device for the whole deployment).

docs.title: Process control (C-02)
docs.text:
• [ ] On a device, run python -m src.config --env through SSH and confirm the printed TESTBED_* values match config.yaml.
  • [ ] Start a tagged process over SSH with the start command of src/common/process_tags.py (for example a sleep 60), close the SSH session, reconnect and run the check command. Expected: running. Run the stop command. Expected: stopped, no process with the tag in ps, PID file removed.

docs.title: Compute load (G-01, J-03)
docs.text:
• [ ] On a device, run python -m src.testbed.load_generator --cpu 50 --duration 60 and watch top or mpstat -P ALL 1. Expected: one core at about 50 % (within 5 points), the others idle.
  • [ ] Run --regime heavy --duration 120 --log /tmp/load.json. Expected: total CPU use between 60 and 80 % of one core, memory in use between 50 and 60 % (free -m), both changing every 10 s; /tmp/load.json lists the drawn targets.
  • [ ] Run --processes 2 --duration 30. Expected: two cores fully busy.

docs.title: Network shaping (G-02, G-03, C-07)
docs.text:
• [ ] On a device, scripts/end_device/apply_latency.sh wlan0 20 20 --once, then ping -c 10 <edge server> from the device. Expected: RTT about 20 ms above the baseline. apply_latency.sh wlan0 --clear restores the baseline.
  • [ ] python -m src.testbed.latency_injector wlan0 --delay 10 --jitter 5 --loss 1 --rate 10, then iperf3 -c <edge server> -t 10 and ping -c 50. Expected: about 10 Mbit/s, RTT 10 ms +- 5 ms, about 1 % loss.
  • [ ] Per destination: --dst <edge server IP> --delay 15 --dst <another device IP> --delay 30. Expected: the two pings differ by about 15 ms.
  • [ ] Note any driver that rejects the HTB tree on wlan0; the single-root fallback (apply_all) is the alternative.

docs.title: Heterogeneity and frequency (G-04, B-04, F-01)
docs.text:
• [ ] Device: sudo python -m src.testbed.heterogeneity freq --max-mhz 600 --state /tmp/f.json, then python -m src.testbed.resource_monitor --output /tmp/m.json --run-id t --node-id d --duration 10. Expected: frequencies_khz at or below 600000 in every sample; freq --restore /tmp/f.json brings them back to 1800000.
  • [ ] Device: sudo python -m src.testbed.heterogeneity cgroup create --name testbed-check --memory-mb 512, then run sh -c "$(python -c 'from src.testbed.heterogeneity import MemoryLimit; print(MemoryLimit().attach_command("testbed-check", "python3 -c \"x=bytearray(700*2**20)\""))')". Expected: the allocation is killed by the OOM killer of the group; cgroup remove cleans up.
  • [ ] Edge server: sudo python -m src.testbed.cpu_frequency apply --state /tmp/s.json, then verify. Expected: governor performance, turbo disabled, every core near the base frequency; restore returns the previous settings.
  • [ ] Device under a long heavy load: the monitor trace shows the temperature and whether throttled ever leaves 0x0; the monitor's own CPU use (top -p <pid>) stays below 2 %.

docs.title: Power and throughput (F-04, F-08, J-07)
docs.text:
• [ ] Device with INA260: pip install -r requirements/power.in, then python -m src.network.power_measurement --interval 0.2 --duration 30 --output /tmp/p.json --run-id t --node-id d. Expected: about 150 samples, idle power 2.5-3.5 W, energy_j consistent with power x 30 s.
  • [ ] Device: python -m src.network.throughput_measurement --server <edge server> --duration 10 --output /tmp/tp.json with iperf3 -s -1 on the edge server, once alone and once with all five devices at the same time. Record the figures (the thesis states 80-120 Mbit/s per device and, in Chapter 5, a measured 19.6 Mbit/s).

docs.title: Partitioned inference and per-phase timing (B-05, D-05)
docs.text:
• [ ] Edge server (data-plane address): python -m src.inference.server --model alexnet --weights models/alexnet.npz --policy SJF --port 5300 --nodes device1,device2,device3,device4. Device: python -m src.inference.client --model alexnet --weights <ed_root>/models/alexnet.npz --server <edge server>:5300 --s 0 --s 4 --s 8 --s 11 --repetitions 10 --output /tmp/phases.json --run-id t --node-id device1. Expected: transmission_ms grows with the transmitted size (s = 1 is the largest cut, s = 8 is 36 KB), remote_ms shrinks with s, s = 11 has no transmission.
  • [ ] Four devices at once with --s 4 and --policy SJF, then --policy RR: the per-device queue_ms values follow the policy (SJF: ascending offloaded work; RR: interleaved), as in the loopback tests.
  • [ ] Compare the measured transmission_ms of the s = 1 cut (1.1 MB) with size / throughput from the iperf3 figure plus the ping RTT.

docs.title: Whole pipeline on the testbed (C-01, C-04, C-13, D-10, D-13)
docs.text:
• [ ] Edge server: scripts/base_station/run_full_benchmarking.sh examples/scenarios/baseline.yaml. Expected: every device runs train_and_run_benchmark.sh both, the three output files appear in results/<run id>/, nodes.json gains statistics, and journal.json shows every entry undone.
  • [ ] Edge server: scripts/base_station/run_experiment.sh examples/scenarios/heavy_load.yaml. During the run, on a device: tc qdisc show dev wlan0 lists the netem (and tbf) queue, top shows the load generator and the monitor; after the run both are gone and tc qdisc show is back to the default. The monitor trace in results/<run id>/monitor/ shows the heavy regime's CPU and memory levels.
  • [ ] Start skew (C-04): in results/<run id>/raw/, compare the origin.wall_time_s of the devices' records. Expected: within the NTP offset (sub-millisecond on the wired management network).
  • [ ] Interrupt a run with Ctrl-C during profiling, then run scripts/base_station/clean_devices.sh. Expected: no testbed- process, no netem queue and no testbed- cgroup remains on any device.
  • [ ] NTP guard: stop chrony on one device and start a run. Expected: the preflight refuses the run with the offending node named.
