docs.title: HeadSplit integration
docs.text:
HeadSplit is the author's separate runtime for head-level partitioning and inter-layer speculation of decoder-only Large Language Models (LLMs) on the five-device cluster (Chapter 6): one controller and four workers, all Raspberry Pis, communicating through PyTorch RPC. The testbed treats it as an optional external runtime: nothing of HeadSplit is imported by the testbed, its code is not vendored, and the integration is command-line only. What the testbed adds is what HeadSplit alone does not have: provisioning of a pinned version on every device, the scenario's network shaping, load and heterogeneity, the monitors and power traces, the run metadata and the results layout. HeadSplit is the first implementation of the runtime plug-in interface (adding_a_runtime.md, src/orchestration/runtimes/headsplit.py), so NNPM configures it in the Create scenario dialog, checks and prepares the devices in the Runtimes dialog and shows its results on the run summary page (nnpm_user_guide.md).

HeadSplit supports Llama-family models (TinyLlama, Llama 3.2 and other models with the Llama attention layout). GPT-2 has a different layout (fused query, key and value projection, learned positions) and is not supported by HeadSplit; the GPT-2 figures of the thesis come from the testbed's own layer-based path (model: gpt2 with the testbed runtime).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
In config.yaml:

headsplit_repo_url: "https://github.com/Dimitrios-Kafetzis/headsplit.git"
headsplit_commit: "4864a22e5bdc2c712ffe071d7f7dba0c3656fb33"   # HeadSplit v0.1.0; null disables HeadSplit
headsplit_dir: null                # directory on the devices; null means <ed_root>/headsplit
headsplit_master_port: 29500

scripts/provision/build_mirror.sh headsplit makes a bare clone at the pinned commit in the mirror and downloads the wheels of HeadSplit's requirements.txt for aarch64 (the devices) and x86_64 (the edge server, for the profile step). HeadSplit keeps its own virtual environment, <headsplit_dir>/.venv, so that its requirements never constrain the testbed's locks. provision_device.sh clones from the mirror, checks out the commit and creates the environment on every device; the same can be done later, device by device, with the Install or update HeadSplit action of NNPM's Runtimes dialog.

The speculation-accuracy profile that the controller needs (artifacts/profile.json) is built once with HeadSplit's scripts/profile_offline.py, which downloads its calibration data (WikiText-103): NNPM's Build the speculation profile action runs it on the edge server (which may reach the internet when allow_upstream is ticked; the devices never do) and copies the result to the controller. The checkpoint (TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 by default) must be on every device: the model catalogue fetches it into bs_models_dir (python -m src.models.weights fetch tinyllama --allow-upstream, see examples/models.yaml), provisioning copies bs_models_dir to the devices, and the Distribute a checkpoint action does the same on demand with checksum verification. The Check the devices button shows all four facts per device: checkout and commit, environment, profile, checkpoint.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A scenario with runtime: headsplit replaces the profiling stage with a HeadSplit run; everything else (apply, collect, teardown, metadata, monitors) is the testbed's:

name: ch6_rtt_sweep
runtime: headsplit
model: tinyllama
devices: [device1, device2, device3, device4, device5]
headsplit:
  controller: device1
  workers: [device2, device3, device4, device5]
  model: TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0
  tokens: 50
  prompt_length: 256
  mode: all                 # headsplit, head_only, layer_based or all
  profile: artifacts/profile.json
network:
  default: {added_rtt_ms: 0}
sweep:
  path: network.default.added_rtt_ms
  values: [0, 5, 10, 20, 40]

Fields: controller and workers name nodes of nodes.json; model is the Hugging Face model name HeadSplit expects; tokens, prompt_length, prompt; mode; profile (relative to the HeadSplit directory); worker_memory_bytes (3 GiB by default), epsilon, alpha_min, memory_replace_threshold, rtt_margin (HeadSplit's placement and speculation parameters, written into the per-run HeadSplit config.yaml); timeout_s; extra_args passed to the controller.

docs.title: What a run does
docs.text:
1. The testbed applies the scenario (shaping, load, heterogeneity, monitors, power) on every named node and writes the metadata, as for any run.
  2. On every worker it starts, as a tagged detached process, scripts/run_worker.py --name workerN --rank N --world-size W --master-addr <controller data-plane address> --master-port <headsplit_master_port> --model <model> from <headsplit_dir>/.venv.
  3. On the controller it writes a per-run HeadSplit config.yaml (the workers by data-plane address and memory, the speculation parameters, the profile path) and runs scripts/run_controller.py --config ... --profile ... --master-addr ... --master-port ... --tokens N --mode <mode>, waiting up to timeout_s. A controller that accepts --json (HeadSplit v0.1.0 and later) also receives --json <results dir>/headsplit_rep<k>.json.
  4. The results come from the JSON file when there is one (the per-mode figures plus the per-token times, the speculation decisions per layer, the placement and the measured round-trip times), otherwise from the controller's summary lines (<mode> total ... ms prefill ... ms decode ... ms/token payload ... MB, with the speculation acceptance and re-placement counts when present, and the speed-up lines). They are written to results/<run id>/headsplit/results.json; the controller and worker logs are kept next to it, and the run summary page shows the per-mode table.
  5. Teardown stops any worker still running and undoes the scenario. Workers exit when the controller shuts the RPC group down, so each repetition starts them afresh.

The aggregation stage does not compute the DNN output files for a HeadSplit run (there is no per-layer profile), and the optimiser is skipped. The monitor and power traces of every device are collected as usual, so energy per token and the energy-delay product can be computed from power/ with src/network/power_measurement.py's energy functions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: examples/scenarios/ch6_rtt_sweep.yaml (one run per added round-trip time) and examples/scenarios/ch6_heterogeneity.yaml (frequency caps and memory limits on the workers) reproduce the Chapter 6 procedures. Without hardware, runtime: headsplit runs in local mode against stub scripts in the tests (tests/integration/test_headsplit_runtime.py), which is how the command lines and the parser are verified; the real runtime is a hardware-checklist item.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Three roles, three lock files. Every dependency is pinned with a hash in requirements/*.lock (generated with scripts/lock_requirements.sh); installing with --require-hashes guarantees the same stack on every machine. The direct dependencies and their minimum versions are in the .in files and follow the software table of Appendix B.

Component Minimum supported Pinned in the lock files (thesis, Appendix B, Table B.1) Operating system Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit (devices), Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (edge server) Bookworm 64-bit on the devices (Python 3.11), Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Python 3.11 3.11 TensorFlow (DNN, Chapter 4) ≥ 2.8.0, CPU 2.15.1 PyTorch (LLM, Chapters 5 and 6) 2.1.2, CPU 2.1.2 (+cpu on x86_64) Transformers 4.36 4.46.3 (Qwen2 needs 4.37, Llama 3.2 needs 4.43, HeadSplit 4.40) scikit-learn ≥ 1.0.0, edge server only 1.9.1 Paramiko (SSH) ≥ 2.11, edge server only 5.1.0 Flask (web application) ≥ 2.2.0, edge server only 3.1.3 NTP client (devices), server (edge server) chrony, configured by provisioning psutil, PyYAML, jsonschema, NumPy 7.2.2, 6.0.3, 4.26.0, 1.26.4

docs.title: Edge server
docs.text:
Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, x86_64. The provisioning script does all of this (and the network services); by hand:

sudo apt-get install -y python3.11 python3.11-venv git rsync iperf3
git clone https://github.com/Dimitrios-Kafetzis/Distributed-Inference-Testbed.git
cd Distributed-Inference-Testbed
python3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r requirements/edge_server.lock \
    --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu   # the CPU build of PyTorch lives there
cp config.example.yaml config.yaml      # then edit
cp nodes.example.json nodes.json        # then edit, or manage through NNPM
.venv/bin/python -m src.config          # shows the effective configuration
.venv/bin/python -m gui.app             # NNPM on nnpm_host:nnpm_port

requirements/edge_server.lock contains TensorFlow and PyTorch (CPU builds): the edge server profiles its own capacity and runs the partitioned-inference service, so it needs the same frameworks as the devices. The x86_64 CPU build of PyTorch (torch==2.1.2+cpu) is published on the PyTorch index, not on PyPI, hence the --extra-index-url (with uv, add --index-strategy unsafe-best-match). With a package mirror in place, replace it with --no-index --find-links mirror/wheels/x86_64.

docs.title: Edge devices
docs.text:
Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm 64-bit (uname -m must print aarch64). scripts/provision/provision_device.sh <node id> installs everything from the mirror; by hand, on the device:

sudo apt-get install -y python3 python3-venv python3-pip chrony iproute2 iperf3 rsync git
mkdir -p ~/testbed && cd ~/testbed
git clone https://github.com/Dimitrios-Kafetzis/Distributed-Inference-Testbed.git code
python3 -m venv venv
venv/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r code/requirements/edge_device.lock       # TensorFlow
venv/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r code/requirements/edge_device_llm.lock   # PyTorch and Transformers (optional)

The directory layout the edge server expects is given by ed_root in config.yaml (default /home/pi/testbed): code/, venv/, models/, data/, results/, run/. The devices need no copy of config.yaml: the edge server passes every setting as TESTBED_* environment variables and command-line arguments.

Optional, for the INA260 power monitor: venv/bin/pip install -r code/requirements/power.in (the Adafruit Blinka and INA260 packages are platform-specific and therefore not in the lock files) and I2C enabled on the board.

Privileges: tc and the heterogeneity module (cpufreq and cgroup writes) run with sudo -n; provisioning installs a sudoers rule that allows exactly those two commands for the device user. Nothing else on a device needs root.

docs.title: Development machine
docs.text:
Any Linux machine with Python 3.11 (this is also what the continuous-integration workflow does):

uv venv .venv --python 3.11
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --require-hashes -r requirements/dev.lock
.venv/bin/pytest -m "not slow"            # fast suite: fakes, dry runs, local mode
.venv/bin/pytest -m slow                  # real TensorFlow and PyTorch models on the CPU
.venv/bin/ruff check . && .venv/bin/mypy && .venv/bin/shellcheck -x $(git ls-files '*.sh')

requirements/dev.lock includes the edge-server stack plus pytest, ruff, mypy and shellcheck. The whole pipeline runs without hardware in local mode:

.venv/bin/python -m src.orchestration.experiment run --scenario examples/scenarios/local_demo.yaml --local
.venv/bin/python -m gui.app --local        # NNPM with simulated nodes

docs.title: Updating the pins
docs.text: Edit the .in files, then scripts/lock_requirements.sh (needs uv), which resolves each lock file for its platform (x86_64-manylinux_2_28 for the edge server and development, aarch64-manylinux_2_28 for the devices) with hashes. Rebuild the mirror afterwards (scripts/provision/build_mirror.sh wheels and manifest).

docs.title: Module reference
docs.text: One entry per module: purpose, command line where the module has one, inputs and outputs. Every command line prints its full help with --help. Device-side tools accept --tag (the process tag that clean_devices.sh uses to find survivors) and, where they produce records, --run-id, --node-id, --origin-wall and --origin-perf (the time origin from the start signal).

docs.title: src/config.py
docs.text: config.yaml with environment-variable overrides (TESTBED_<KEY>), validated against docs/schemas/config.schema.json; secrets only from the environment. python -m src.config [--config FILE] [--env] prints the effective configuration as JSON, or as TESTBED_* assignments for scripts.

docs.title: src/common/nodes.py
docs.text: nodes.json: Node (id, role Base Station or End Device, data-plane and management addresses, coordinates, statistics), Topology (at most one edge server), load, validate and save atomically; TESTBED_NODES selects another file. Imports the earlier release's format.

docs.title: Common infrastructure (src/common/)
docs.text: Module Purpose runner.py CommandRunner protocol with SubprocessRunner, FakeRunner (scripted replies, records calls) and DryRunRunner (prints the commands) clock.py injectable clocks; perf_counter_ns for intervals, the wall clock only for the start-signal origin sysfs.py rooted access to /sys, /proc and cgroupfs (a temporary tree in tests) process_tags.py detached tagged processes: setsid process groups, PID files, TESTBED_TAG, stop by group and by tag runs.py run ids, the results layout (RunPaths), atomic JSON writes, the run journal (RunJournal: record, undo in reverse order, pending entries after a restart) seeds.py seed_everything(seed) for random, NumPy, TensorFlow, PyTorch and PYTHONHASHSEED start_signal.py wait_until(T0) and the captured origin; python -m src.common.start_signal --start-at T0 metadata.py metadata.json: scenario, Git commit, framework versions, per-node facts, before any device command probe.py python -m src.common.probe [--no-frameworks]: the node's hostname, kernel, OS, Python, framework versions, CPU model, cores, maximum frequency, memory, NTP status, as JSON

docs.title: transport.py
docs.text: ParamikoTransport (SSH), LocalTransport (local subprocesses in per-node directories), FakeTransport (tests). Line streaming, exit status, failure classes (authentication, unreachable, command), file fetch.

docs.title: ssh_executor.py
docs.text: Concurrent remote commands with a merged [node][stream] log streamed to subscribers; aborts the experiment on the first failure unless told otherwise. python -m src.network.ssh_executor "<command>" <node id or last octet>... [--log FILE] [--no-abort] [--timeout S] [--nodes-file FILE] [--local].

docs.title: collection.py
docs.text: Result files from the devices into the run directory: push through scripts/end_device/transfer_files.sh (scp with the hostname prefixed), or pull through the transport.

docs.title: latency_measurement.py (device)
docs.text: Ping latency to the edge server and other nodes plus a psutil snapshot of memory and CPU, written as a latency record. python -m src.network.latency_measurement --target ID=IP ... --count N --output FILE --run-id R --node-id D [--interface wlan0] [--interval S] [--timeout S].

docs.title: node_statistics.py (edge server)
docs.text: Per-node averages of the latency records into final_latencies_averages.json, and the statistics in nodes.json. python -m src.network.node_statistics <latency dir> <output> [--nodes nodes.json] [--run-id ID].

docs.title: power_measurement.py (device)
docs.text: INA260 current, voltage and power at an interval into a PowerTrace; energy functions (total energy, energy per inference or per token, energy-delay product). python -m src.network.power_measurement --interval S --duration S --output FILE --run-id R --node-id D [--address 0x40] [--fake].

docs.title: throughput_measurement.py (device)
docs.text: iperf3 throughput to the edge server, as a ThroughputResult. python -m src.network.throughput_measurement --server IP --duration S --output FILE [--parallel N] [--reverse] [--udp --bitrate 50M] [--port P] [--bind IP].

docs.title: records.py
docs.text: The latency-and-system record type.

docs.title: load_generator.py (device)
docs.text: Deterministic CPU and memory contention: a duty-cycle loop per worker for a CPU percentage, 1 KB blocks held for a memory percentage; modes fixed, continuous (seeded redraw every cycle), --regime light|moderate|heavy (the Chapter 3 ranges) and --processes N (the Chapter 4 model). python -m src.testbed.load_generator [--cpu % --memory %] [--cores N] [--mode fixed|continuous --cpu-range MIN MAX --memory-range MIN MAX] [--regime R] [--processes N] [--period-ms MS] [--cycle-s S] [--duration S] [--seed N] [--log FILE]. Releases everything on SIGTERM.

docs.title: latency_injector.py (device)
docs.text: tc-netem shaping on an interface: delay with variation modes constant, uniform, square, jitter, loss, a token-bucket rate cap, per-destination leaves under an HTB root. python -m src.testbed.latency_injector <iface> [--delay MS | --delay MIN MAX --mode M --period S] [--jitter MS] [--loss %] [--rate MBPS] [--dst IP ...] [--duration S] [--seed N] [--clear] [--no-sudo] [--dry-run]. scripts/end_device/apply_latency.sh keeps the historical command line.

docs.title: background_traffic.py
docs.text: Builds the iperf3 stream command for a device (UDP or TCP at a target rate); the orchestrator starts it.

docs.title: heterogeneity.py (device, sudo)
docs.text: freq --max-mhz N (cpufreq cap, with --state FILE to record and --restore STATE to revert), cgroup create --name N --memory-mb M and cgroup remove --name N (cgroups v2), threads --count N (environment for the inference runtime). --sysfs-root for tests.

docs.title: resource_monitor.py (device)
docs.text: The 1 Hz monitoring agent: CPU, memory, temperature, per-core frequency, throttling flags, as a ResourceTrace. python -m src.testbed.resource_monitor --output FILE --run-id R --node-id D [--interval S] [--duration S] [--nominal-khz K].

docs.title: cpu_frequency.py (edge server, sudo)
docs.text: Nominal frequency policy: performance governor, turbo off, maximum frequency at the base frequency; apply --state FILE, verify, restore --state FILE.

docs.title: registry.py
docs.text: The adapter interface (a model as S stages with FLOPs, MACs and output size per stage) and the name registry; plug-ins through TESTBED_MODEL_MODULES or the testbed.models entry-point group. An adapter's PARAMETERS (a JSON Schema) describes its constructor arguments: parameter_schema(name), validate_model_args(name, args) (the scenario's model_args), parse_model_args(text) (the tools' --model-args). See adding_a_model.md.

docs.title: tf/ (TensorFlow, CPU)
docs.text: alexnet.py (the 11 stages of Chapter 4, 227 × 227 × 3 input), vgg16.py (eight stages), resnet50.py (six stages cut at the residual-stage boundaries), gru_qoe.py (the Chapter 4 QoE predictor: GRU, attention, output), on keras_stages.py (sequential and functional-cut adapters, analytical operation counts, .npz weights; select_cuts(model) for adapters that compute their cuts). keras_applications.py: any tf.keras.applications classifier (keras_app with application, and the registered names mobilenetv2, efficientnetb0, densenet121, resnet50v2, inceptionv3, nasnetmobile, xception), cut where a single tensor crosses the graph (find_single_tensor_cuts) and thinned to max_stages stages of comparable work (thin_cuts).

docs.title: torch/ (PyTorch, CPU)
docs.text: decoder.py (decoder-only LLMs as stages: embedding, layers, LM head; the cut is the hidden state; the FAMILIES table gives the attribute names and structural facts of GPT-2, Llama, Mistral, Qwen2 and Gemma), gpt2.py, tinyllama.py, hf_decoder.py (hf_decoder: any checkpoint or configuration of a known family; llama32_1b, qwen25_05b), headwise.py (per-head decomposition of a decoder layer: head units, projection, FFN, equal to the stock layer; follows the family table), hooks.py (python -m src.models.torch.hooks --model NAME --seq-len T --repetitions N --output FILE [--weights DIR] [--config JSON]: per-block timing with forward hooks).

docs.title: inputs.py
docs.text: Input sources (synthetic, numpy_file, image_file, image_folder, text_prompt): load_sample(spec, adapter, seed, data_dir) returns the array, a label when the source has one, and a description that the measurement record keeps. The tools take the spec as --input-source JSON.

docs.title: weights.py
docs.text: The model catalogue <bs_models_dir>/models.yaml (example: examples/models.yaml): python -m src.models.weights list|verify|checksums|fetch [--models-dir DIR] [NAME ...] [--all] [--allow-upstream]. Kinds: npz (seeded weights), keras_imagenet (the ImageNet weights of a Keras application), hf_checkpoint (a Hugging Face snapshot). SHA256SUMS files make every copy verifiable; fetch is the only command that reaches the internet.

docs.title: fake.py
docs.text: A model with configurable stage costs for tests and local mode.

docs.title: flops.py
docs.text: Analytical operation counts (FLOPs = 2 × MACs) from layer configuration and shapes.

docs.title: profiler.py
docs.text: Stage-by-stage execution with perf_counter_ns, a sampler for peak CPU (from CPU-time deltas over windows of at least 20 ms, clipped to 100 % × cores) and peak resident memory, cumulative values per partition point.

docs.title: inference.py (device)
docs.text: python -m src.models.inference {prepare,benchmark,partial,complete,capacity,verify} ...: prepare the weights and the test image with a seed; benchmark across all partition points into BenchmarkResults files; run stages 1..s (partial) or s+1..S (complete) on a tensor file; report FLOP/s; verify compares every partition point with the unpartitioned model (maximum deviation, top-1 agreement, accuracy when the input has a label) and exits with status 1 above --tolerance. Every mode takes --model-args JSON and --input-source JSON. scripts/end_device/train_and_run_benchmark.sh <train|benchmark|both> <model dir> <model> <output dir> [options] wraps it.

docs.title: server.py (edge server)
docs.text: The inference service: receives offloaded requests, orders them under RR or SJF, runs stages s+1..S, acknowledges every request when its last byte arrives, returns the output with the server-side timestamps. python -m src.inference.server --model M [--weights W] --policy RR|SJF --port P [--host H] [--nodes d1,d2,...] [--max-requests N].

docs.title: client.py (device)
docs.text: Partitioned inference with per-phase timing (local, transmission, remote, queue wait) into a phases record. python -m src.inference.client --model M [--weights W] --server HOST:PORT --s S [--s S ...] --repetitions N --output FILE --run-id R --node-id D.

docs.title: scheduler.py, protocol.py
docs.text: The pure RR and SJF schedulers; the length-prefixed JSON-plus-payload wire protocol (request, ack, result, error).

docs.title: benchmark_results.py
docs.text: BenchmarkResults, ResourceTrace, PowerTrace and their JSON Schema; python -m src.benchmarking.benchmark_results FILE validates a record.

docs.title: result_aggregation.py
docs.text: Per-device averages over repetitions and trace merging. python -m src.benchmarking.result_aggregation <raw dir> <output> [--monitor-dir D] [--power-dir D] [--merged-dir D].

docs.title: partition_calculator.py
docs.text: Maximum feasible partition point per device (memory and CPU constraints). python -m src.benchmarking.partition_calculator <final_latencies_averages.json> <total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json> <output>.

docs.title: stats.py
docs.text: Mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, 95th percentile, count.

docs.title: delay_model.py
docs.text: Local (measured or analytical), transmission (size_over_rate or rtt_only) and remote (RR or SJF) delay per device; total delay and variance of a vector.

docs.title: algorithms/
docs.text: greedy.py (single-step moves, Chapter 4), exhaustive.py (enumeration with the optimality gap), trend_based.py (linear trends over num_solutions neighbours); a registry with plug-ins.

docs.title: delay_optimizer.py
docs.text: python -m src.partitioning.delay_optimizer <max points> <total averages> <latencies> --scheduling_algorithm SJF|RR --mode default|optimize|exhaustive_search|trend_based_optimize [--algorithm NAME] --objective total_delay|variance [--partition_scheme '[3,5,8,1]'|'{"device1": 3}'|50% --partition_scheme_mode explicit|percentage] [--max_total_delays '[150,150]'] [--output-dir DIR] [--log_file FILE] [--edge-capacity FLOPS] [--rr-quantum-ms MS] [--transmission-mode M] [--throughput-file FILE] [--nodes d1,d2] [--scenario FILE]. Writes optimized_partition_scheme.json and search_log.txt.

docs.title: experiment.py
docs.text: The pipeline (preflight, apply, profile, collect, aggregate, optimise, teardown) and the benchmarking subset. python -m src.orchestration.experiment run|benchmark|plan --scenario FILE | --name NAME [--version N] [--local [ROOT] --devices N] [--results-dir DIR] [--run-id ID] [--allow-dirty]; teardown [--local [ROOT]] undoes the pending entries of unfinished runs. plan prints the command plan without running anything. The scripts scripts/base_station/run_experiment.sh, run_full_benchmarking.sh and clean_devices.sh wrap these.

docs.title: scenario.py
docs.text: Schema validation with defaults, the versioned ScenarioStore, sweep expansion, per-node overlays, content hashes.

docs.title: local_mode.py
docs.text: create_local_testbed(root, devices): the simulated testbed on one machine.

docs.title: geo.py
docs.text: calculate_distance (Haversine) and calculate_latency (5 ms + 1 ms/km, clipped to [5, 50] ms), re-exported by gui/app.py.

docs.title: runtimes/
docs.text: The runtime plug-in interface (Runtime: scenario block schema, run, check_node, actions and perform, results; ActionSession; the registry with TESTBED_RUNTIME_MODULES and the testbed.runtimes entry-point group), testbed.py (the built-in profile stage) and headsplit.py (HeadSplit: commands, readiness checks, the install, profile and checkpoint actions, the JSON and summary-line parsers). headsplit_runtime.py keeps the earlier import path. See adding_a_runtime.md and headsplit_integration.md.

docs.title: Provisioning support (src/provisioning/)
docs.text: render.py (python -m src.provisioning.render --role edge-server|device [--node ID] [--out DIR] [--vars] [--var K=V]), networks.py (prefix to network, DHCP pool, 802.11ac channel helpers), mirror.py (python -m src.provisioning.mirror manifest|verify [--mirror DIR]). The scripts are described in ../scripts/provision/README.md.

docs.title: NNPM (gui/)
docs.text: app.py (python -m gui.app [--host H] [--port P] [--config FILE] [--nodes-file FILE] [--local [ROOT]] [--devices N] [--allow-dirty]; the nnpm console script), state.py (the prober, the run manager with sweeps, the task manager, the application state), blueprints/ (topology, status, scenarios, runs with the summary page, optimise, catalog, runtimes), templates/run.html (the run summary page). See nnpm_user_guide.md.

docs.title: Shell scripts
docs.text: Script Where Purpose scripts/base_station/run_full_benchmarking.sh [scenario] [--local [ROOT]] edge server the four-stage benchmarking pipeline (default scenario examples/scenarios/baseline.yaml) scripts/base_station/run_experiment.sh <scenario.yaml \| --name NAME [--version N]> [--local [ROOT]] edge server a full experiment scripts/base_station/clean_devices.sh [--local [ROOT]] edge server stop every tagged process, clear shaping and cgroups, undo pending journals scripts/end_device/train_and_run_benchmark.sh <train\|benchmark\|both> <model dir> <model> <output dir> [options] device prepare the weights and the test input, run the benchmark, or both scripts/end_device/transfer_files.sh <user> <edge server> <directory> <files...> device scp the result files with the hostname prefixed scripts/end_device/apply_latency.sh <iface> <min> <max> [--once\|--continuous\|--periodic] ... \| --clear device the historical tc-netem wrapper scripts/provision/*.sh edge server, device provisioning (see its README) scripts/lock_requirements.sh [--upgrade] development regenerate the lock files

docs.title: NNPM tutorial
docs.text:
A walk through every function of the Neural Network Architecture Partitioning (NNPM) manager, with screenshots. The screenshots were taken in local mode, where every node is simulated on one machine, so you can follow every step on a laptop without the testbed; on the hardware the same screens show the real devices. The NNPM user guide is the reference for each screen; this tutorial is the guided tour.

The screenshots are produced by scripts/docs/nnpm_screenshots.py (Playwright, requirements/docs.in), so they stay in step with the application.

docs.title: 1. Start NNPM
docs.text:
Without hardware:

uv venv .venv --python 3.11
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --require-hashes -r requirements/dev.lock
.venv/bin/python -m gui.app --local --devices 5

Open http://127.0.0.1:8001/. On the edge server, provisioning installs nnpm.service, so NNPM is already running at http://<edge server management address>:8001/; to start it by hand, run .venv/bin/python -m gui.app there. To require a login, set nnpm_basic_auth_env in config.yaml to the name of an environment variable holding user:password.

docs.title: 2. The main view
docs.text:
Three areas:

  • Toolbar: Edit network, Add node by clicking the map, Create scenario, Run experiment, Benchmarking, Optimise, Runtimes, Stop; the "Draw links" box; the run indicator (idle, or the current run id with running); the local mode badge when every node is simulated.
  • Map: one marker per node of nodes.json. The edge server (Base Station in the software) has a differently coloured marker. The label under a marker shows the node id, its data-plane address and a dot: green when the last reachability probe got three replies out of three pings, red otherwise, grey before the first probe. A probe round starts every two seconds. The red lines join every pair of nodes; hovering one shows the distance and the synthetic link latency (5 ms plus 1 ms per kilometre, clipped to 5 to 50 ms).
  • Side panel: the Node panel (details of the clicked marker) and the Runs panel (the runs in the results directory, newest first).
  • Terminal (below): the merged log of the running experiment, one line per device output, tagged [node][stream]; the Filter box keeps one node's lines; Clear empties the panel.

docs.title: 3. Nodes: inspect, edit, add
docs.text:
Click a marker. The Node panel shows the role, both addresses, the reachability and, after a benchmarking run, the last measured latency, available memory and CPU usage of the device, with the time and the run that produced them.

Edit network lists every node with Edit and Delete buttons and a form for a new node (id, role, data-plane address, management address, coordinates). Saving writes nodes.json, the single source of truth that the command-line scripts read too.

Add node by clicking the map: press the button (it stays highlighted), click the map where the device stands; the form opens with the clicked coordinates filled in. Enter the id and the addresses and save; the marker appears at once and the prober includes the node in its next round.

Markers are draggable: moving one saves the new coordinates, and the link latencies derived from the distances follow.

docs.title: 4. Create a scenario
docs.text:
A scenario holds every parameter of an experiment. The dialog saves it as a version (scenarios/<name>/v<N>.json) that can be run again later, identically.

From top to bottom:

  1. Name, runtime, model. The runtime is testbed by default (per-layer profiling and partitioned inference); an external runtime such as HeadSplit replaces the profile stage (section 9). The model list comes from the registry: the thesis models (alexnet, vgg16, resnet50, gru_qoe, gpt2, tinyllama), the generic adapters (mobilenetv2, efficientnetb0, densenet121, keras_app, llama32_1b, qwen25_05b, hf_decoder) and fake for local mode.
  2. Repetitions, warm-up, seed, edge-server policy (SJF or RR), settling time, and the optional partitioned inference at a list of partition points.
  3. Model parameters: shown when the chosen model declares some (here the fake model's input size and time scale; for a Keras model the number of classes, for a decoder the sequence length, for keras_app the application name, for hf_decoder the checkpoint). They are saved as model_args.
  4. Sweep: a field path and comma-separated values make one run per value, run one after the other (edge_server.policy with RR, SJF in the screenshot; network.default.added_rtt_ms with 0, 5, 10, 20 is the Chapter 6 study).
  5. Per node, one block per end device with a selection box: link delay (typed, or filled by Derive latencies from the map), variation (constant, uniform redraw, square wave) with its range and period, jitter, loss, bandwidth cap; load mode (none, fixed CPU and memory percentages, a regime of the thesis, backlogged processes); maximum CPU frequency, memory limit, threads. Shaping is applied with tc-netem on the device's data-plane interface at launch and removed at the end; the load generator runs for the whole run.

Save scenario stores the version; Save and run also starts it and shows the run id in the toolbar indicator.

docs.title: 5. Run an experiment and follow it
docs.text:
Run experiment picks a saved scenario version and starts it. Benchmarking is the shortcut for the four-stage profiling pipeline of Appendix B (model, repetitions, warm-up, seed; the devices whose last probe was green are preselected; no load or shaping):

While a run is in progress the indicator turns orange, the Runs panel lists the run as running, and the terminal shows the devices' output as it arrives: the metadata probe, the per-node commands, the profiler's progress, the collection and the aggregation.

When the run finishes the indicator shows completed (or aborted with the reason), the Runs panel updates, and the node statistics measured by the run appear in the Node panel.

Stop aborts the running experiment at its next stage boundary. Every change recorded in the run journal is undone in reverse order (processes stopped, shaping cleared, frequencies restored, cgroups removed); the run directory keeps what was produced so far. A sweep stops as well: its queued runs are abandoned.

docs.title: 6. The run summary page
docs.text:
The run id in the Runs panel opens /runs/<run id>:

The page shows the scenario (name and version, pipeline, runtime, model, devices), the outputs (the edge server's measured capacity, the optimised partition vector and its objective), the three output files of the thesis with download links (total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json, calculated_max_partition_points.json, final_latencies_averages.json), the metadata, summary, journal and merged log, every other file of the run directory, and the last lines of the log. The JSON button returns the same as data (GET /api/runs/<id>).

docs.title: 7. Optimise
docs.text:
Optimise runs the partition optimiser on a finished profiling run without re-running anything on the devices: choose the run, the algorithm (greedy, exhaustive, trend-based, or a plug-in), the edge-server scheduling policy (RR or SJF), the objective (total delay or variance), the initial partition (50% of the model depth, an explicit list, or a {node: s} mapping), an optional maximum total delay per device and the transmission model (round-trip time only, or cut size over the measured rate plus latency).

The result is the partition vector with the objective value and the all-local baseline, and a table per device (partition point, local, transmission, remote and total delay). It is written under results/<run id>/optimisation/<timestamp>-nnpm/ with the scenario version, the hashes of its inputs and the search log.

docs.title: 8. Sweeps
docs.text: A scenario with a sweep runs once per value. The Runs panel shows every run with its value; each run's summary page has the Sweep table: one row per value with the run id, its status and its main figure (the optimised total delay and vector for the testbed runtime, the per-mode totals for HeadSplit).

docs.title: 9. HeadSplit and other runtimes
docs.text:
Selecting the headsplit runtime in Create scenario adds the HeadSplit block, rendered from the runtime's own schema: the controller (a device), the workers (check boxes), the Hugging Face model, tokens, prompt length, mode (headsplit, head_only, layer_based, all), the speculation parameters and the time-out. The per-node shaping, load and heterogeneity blocks stay available, since the Chapter 6 studies combine them with HeadSplit.

Before the first HeadSplit run, the devices need the runtime, its speculation profile and the checkpoint. The Runtimes dialog shows whether they have them and prepares them:

  • Check the devices runs the runtime's readiness checks on every node through the same connections as experiments: for HeadSplit the checkout and its commit against headsplit_commit, the environment (torch and transformers import from HeadSplit's own virtual environment), the speculation profile on the controller, and the checkpoint in the devices' models directory (the model field changes which checkpoint is looked for). Green, amber, red; hover a cell for the detail.
  • Install or update HeadSplit clones or updates the runtime from the mirror at the pinned commit and builds its environment on the selected devices.
  • Build the speculation profile runs HeadSplit's profile_offline.py on the edge server (tick allow_upstream: the calibration data is downloaded) and copies the profile to the controller.
  • Distribute a checkpoint copies bs_models_dir/<model directory> to the selected devices and verifies the checksums there (the model catalogue, python -m src.models.weights fetch tinyllama --allow-upstream, puts the checkpoint in bs_models_dir first).

Actions run as tasks: one at a time, never while an experiment runs; their log goes to the terminal tagged [task], and Stop ends a running task after its current step.

The summary page of a HeadSplit run has the HeadSplit results table: per mode the total, prefill and decode times, the payload, the speculation acceptance, the re-placements and the speed-up over layer-based partitioning, from the controller's JSON results (HeadSplit v0.1.0 and later) or its summary lines.

Any other runtime registered through the plug-in interface (adding_a_runtime.md) appears in the same two drop-downs with its own block, checks and actions.

docs.title: 10. Local mode as a rehearsal
docs.text: Everything above works in local mode: the fake model profiles in milliseconds, shaping and load run in dry-run mode, the HeadSplit checks and actions run against the directory named by headsplit_dir on this machine (the install action prints the plan it would run). Rehearse a scenario in local mode, then run the saved version on the hardware: the scenario file is the same.

docs.title: 11. Scripting NNPM
docs.text:
Every dialog is backed by an HTTP interface, so a shell script or a notebook can do what the dialogs do (nnpm_user_guide.md lists every route):

BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8001

# Save a scenario version and start it.
curl -s -X POST $BASE/api/scenarios -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d @examples/scenarios/baseline.yaml.json      # a scenario as JSON
curl -s -X POST $BASE/api/runs -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"name": "baseline", "version": 1}'
# Follow the log (server-sent events) and read the result.
curl -sN $BASE/events/runs/<run id>
curl -s $BASE/api/runs/<run id> | python -m json.tool
# Readiness of the devices for HeadSplit, then an action.
curl -s "$BASE/api/runtimes/headsplit/status?model=TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0"
curl -s -X POST $BASE/api/runtimes/headsplit/actions/checkpoint \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"nodes": ["device1", "device2"]}'

The command-line scripts (scripts/base_station/run_experiment.sh, run_full_benchmarking.sh, clean_devices.sh) use the same scenario files and write the same run directories, so runs started from either side appear in the Runs panel.

docs.title: NNPM user guide
docs.text: The Neural Network Architecture Partitioning (NNPM) manager is the web application that configures the testbed and runs experiments. It is served from the edge server and used from any browser on the management network. This is the reference per screen; the NNPM tutorial is the guided tour with screenshots.

docs.title: Starting NNPM
docs.text:
On the edge server (after installation):

.venv/bin/python -m gui.app                # nnpm_host:nnpm_port from config.yaml (default port 8001)
.venv/bin/python -m gui.app --local        # a demonstration with simulated nodes, on this machine

Provisioning installs nnpm.service, so NNPM is normally already running at http://<edge server management address>:8001/. Flask's debug mode is off; --debug exists for development on a laptop only. To require a login, set nnpm_basic_auth_env in config.yaml to the name of an environment variable holding user:password; NNPM then asks for HTTP basic authentication.

docs.title: The main view
docs.text:
The page has three parts: the toolbar, the map with the side panel, and the terminal.

Map. One marker per node of nodes.json, the edge server included (its marker is drawn in a different colour). The label under a marker shows the node id, its data-plane address and a coloured dot: green when the last reachability probe received three replies out of three pings, red otherwise, grey before the first probe. A background prober pings every node concurrently and starts a new round every two seconds (probe_period_s); a slow or unreachable node keeps its last colour until its probe answers. Red lines join every pair of markers; hovering a line shows the distance between the two nodes and the synthetic latency of the link (5 ms plus 1 ms per kilometre, clipped to 5 to 50 ms). The "Draw links" box hides them.

The map tiles come from map_tiles_url; on an isolated network set map_offline: true and the map draws a plain grid instead of fetching tiles. Leaflet is served by NNPM itself, so the application never needs internet access.

Node panel. Clicking a marker shows the node's role, addresses, reachability, and the statistics of the last benchmarking run: average ping latency, available memory and CPU usage with the time of the measurement and the run that produced them. The panel also has Edit and Delete buttons.

Runs panel. The runs found in the results directory, newest first, with their scenario name and status. The run id links to the run's summary, from which every result file can be downloaded (/api/runs/<id>/files/<path>).

Terminal. The merged log of the running experiment: every line is tagged [node][stream] and appears as it is produced on the device. The filter box keeps the lines of one node; Clear empties the panel. Lines that NNPM writes itself are tagged [nnpm].

docs.title: Editing the topology
docs.text:
• Add node by clicking the map: press the button (it stays highlighted), click the map at the desired position; the add dialog opens with the clicked coordinates. Enter the id, the role, the data-plane address and, with a separate management network, the management address. Saving writes nodes.json; the marker appears at once and the prober includes the node in its next round.
  • Edit network: a table of all nodes with Edit and Delete buttons, and the same form for a new node.
  • Dragging a marker moves the node and saves the new coordinates. The links and the derived latencies follow.

nodes.json is the single source of truth: the command-line scripts read the same file.

docs.title: Create scenario
docs.text:
The dialog captures every parameter of an experiment and saves it as a scenario version (scenarios/<name>/v<N>.json, see scenario_reference.md).

Top part: name, runtime, model, repetitions, warm-up passes, seed, the edge server's scheduling policy (SJF or RR), the settling time, and optionally partitioned inference at a list of partition points.

  • Runtime. testbed is the per-layer profiling and partitioned-inference path. An external runtime such as headsplit adds its own block below the top part, rendered from the runtime's schema: for HeadSplit the controller (a device drop-down), the workers (check boxes), the Hugging Face model, tokens, prompt length, mode, the speculation parameters and the time-out. The per-node shaping, load and heterogeneity blocks stay available, since the Chapter 6 studies combine them with HeadSplit. See headsplit_integration.md.
  • Model parameters. A model with parameters (the number of classes of a Keras model, the sequence length of a decoder, the application name of keras_app, the checkpoint of hf_decoder) shows them under the model drop-down; they are saved as model_args.
  • Sweep. A field path (for example network.default.added_rtt_ms or edge_server.policy) and comma-separated values make one run per value. NNPM runs them one after the other; the Runs panel shows every run with its value, and each run's summary page has the sweep table.

Per node (one block per end device, each with a selection box):

  • link delay in milliseconds, typed or filled by Derive latencies from the map (the rule's value for the link to the edge server, constant mode); variation (constant, uniform redraw within a range every period, square wave); jitter; loss; bandwidth cap. These are applied with tc-netem on the device's data-plane interface at launch and removed at the end;
  • load mode: none, fixed (CPU percentage of one core and memory percentage), regime (light, moderate, heavy: the Chapter 3 ranges) or backlogged processes (the Chapter 4 model); the load generator runs on the node for the whole run;
  • heterogeneity: maximum CPU frequency, memory limit, thread count.

Save scenario stores the version; Save and run also starts the run and returns at once with a run id, which appears in the toolbar indicator. All per-node actions are issued concurrently through one SSH session per node.

docs.title: Run experiment
docs.text: Choose a saved scenario version and run it. The same scenario can be run again later, identically, which is what versioning is for.

docs.title: Run summary page
docs.text: The run id in the Runs panel opens /runs/<run id>: the scenario (name and version, runtime, model, devices, sweep value), the outputs (edge-server capacity, optimised vector and objective, HeadSplit totals), the three output files of the thesis with download links and every other file, the runtime's results (for HeadSplit a table per mode: total, prefill, decode time per token, payload, speculation acceptance, re-placements, speed-up versus layer-based), the other runs of the same sweep (one row per value with the main figure), and the last lines of the merged log. GET /api/runs/<run id> returns the same as JSON.

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
The Runtimes dialog shows, for a chosen runtime, whether the devices are ready for it and lets you prepare them. Check the devices runs the runtime's readiness checks on every node through the same connections as experiments and shows them as a table (green, amber, red; hover a cell for the detail). For HeadSplit: the checkout and its commit against headsplit_commit, the environment (torch and transformers import from <headsplit_dir>/.venv), the speculation profile on the controller, and the checkpoint under the devices' models directory (type a model name to look for another checkpoint).

Below the table, one form per maintenance action. For HeadSplit: Install or update HeadSplit (clone or update from the mirror at the pinned commit and build the environment on the selected devices), Build the speculation profile (HeadSplit's profile_offline.py on the edge server, then a copy to the controller; the calibration data is downloaded, so allow_upstream must be ticked and the edge server must reach the internet), Distribute a checkpoint (from bs_models_dir/<model directory> to the selected devices, verified with SHA256SUMS there; the catalogue, python -m src.models.weights, fetches checkpoints into bs_models_dir). Actions run as tasks: one at a time, never while an experiment runs, with their log in the terminal tagged [task]; Stop ends a running task after its current step. See adding_a_runtime.md for the interface behind the dialog.

docs.title: Benchmarking
docs.text: The Benchmarking dialog (model, repetitions, warm-up, seed) runs the four-stage profiling pipeline across the active devices: dispatch of train_and_run_benchmark.sh both, result collection, post-processing (latency measurement, aggregation, feasibility) and the three output files total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json, calculated_max_partition_points.json and final_latencies_averages.json in results/<run id>/. The devices whose last probe was green are preselected; before the first probe, every registered device takes part. No load or shaping is applied.

docs.title: Optimise
docs.text: The Optimise dialog loads a profiling run and runs the partition optimiser on it: algorithm (greedy, exhaustive, trend-based, or a plug-in), edge-server scheduling policy (RR or SJF), objective (total delay or variance), initial partition (50% of the model depth, an explicit list, or a {node: s} mapping), optional maximum total delay per device, and the transmission model (round-trip time only, or cut size over the measured rate plus latency). The result is shown as a table (device, s, local, transmission, remote and total delay) with the all-local baseline, and written to results/<run id>/optimisation/<timestamp>-nnpm/ together with the scenario version, the hashes of the input files and the search log.

docs.title: Stop
docs.text: Stop aborts the running experiment: the pipeline stops at the next stage boundary, every journal entry is undone in reverse order (processes stopped, shaping cleared, frequencies restored, cgroups removed) and the run is marked aborted. The run directory keeps everything produced so far. scripts/base_station/clean_devices.sh does the same from the command line, also for runs interrupted by a crash or a restart.

docs.title: Local mode
docs.text: python -m gui.app --local [ROOT] [--devices N] creates a simulated testbed under ROOT (default .local_testbed): an edge server and N devices as working directories on this machine, with the fake model, dry-run shaping and a fake /sys tree. Every dialog works; the terminal shows the same log a real run produces. The page shows a "local mode" badge. The Runtimes dialog works too: the HeadSplit checks run against headsplit_dir on this machine, the install action prints the plan it would run (--dry-run), the profile action runs the profile script found there, and a checkpoint is copied between local directories.

docs.title: Interface summary (for scripts)

docs.title: Provisioning scripts
docs.text:
Bash scripts that take the testbed from blank microSD cards to provisioned nodes. They read config.yaml and nodes.json through src/provisioning/render.py; no address, user name or path is written in a script. Every script accepts --dry-run, which prints the state-changing commands instead of running them (read-only queries such as uname -m over SSH still run), and every step is idempotent: a file is installed only when its content differs, an environment is created only when absent. Elapsed times are appended to results/provisioning/timing.log.

Order of operations on a new testbed:

  1. On the edge server: copy config.example.yaml to config.yaml and nodes.example.json to nodes.json, edit both, export the access-point passphrase in the variable named by ap_passphrase_env, then scripts/provision/provision_edge_server.sh --allow-upstream. This installs the packages, the access point (hostapd), DHCP and DNS for both networks (dnsmasq), the NTP server (chrony), the static management address, the mirror service and the NNPM service, and creates the Python environment from requirements/edge_server.lock.
  2. scripts/provision/build_mirror.sh wheels (and headsplit when headsplit_commit is set, models when bs_models_dir/models.yaml exists): the wheels of every lock file go to mirror/wheels/<arch>/, HeadSplit's wheels for both architectures and its bare clone to mirror/wheels/*-headsplit/ and mirror/src/, the model catalogue's weights to mirror/models/.
  3. For each device: flash the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm image, mount its boot partition and run scripts/provision/prepare_image.sh <node id> <boot mountpoint>. Boot the device on the management switch; it registers under its nodes.json management address.
  4. Once, with the first device booted: scripts/provision/build_mirror.sh apt <node id> fetches the Debian packages through that device into mirror/apt/, then build_mirror.sh manifest writes mirror/MANIFEST.json.
  5. For each device: scripts/provision/provision_device.sh <node id> [--llm]. From then on the device installs only from the mirror.
Script Runs on Purpose prepare_image.sh edge server, card mounted first-boot custom.toml: hostname, user and SSH key, WiFi, time zone provision_edge_server.sh edge server packages, SSH key, access point, DHCP/DNS, NTP server, mirror and NNPM services, Python environment build_mirror.sh edge server the only script that contacts upstream sources; builds the versioned mirror provision_device.sh edge server provisions one device over SSH; calls device_setup.sh on it device_setup.sh device the device-side steps: hostname, apt, chrony, sudoers, pip, venv, headsplit, verify, network lib.sh both shared helpers (run, remote, install_file, load_variables, timing_log)

Templates are in templates/ and rendered by python -m src.provisioning.render; the rendered files for the example configuration are kept as golden files under tests/golden/provision/. The mirror layout and manifest are described in src/provisioning/mirror.py.

docs.title: Pinned dependencies
docs.text:
The .in files list direct dependencies with their minimum supported versions. The .lock files pin every package to an exact version with hashes (the versions listed in the thesis software table, Appendix B, Table B.1), per role and platform, and are what gets installed:

Lock file Role Platform edge_server.lock edge server (NNPM, SSH dispatch, aggregation, optimiser, model profiling) x86_64, Python 3.11 edge_device.lock edge device, DNN experiments (TensorFlow) aarch64, Python 3.11 edge_device_llm.lock edge device, LLM experiments (PyTorch, Transformers) aarch64, Python 3.11 dev.lock development and continuous integration x86_64, Python 3.11 docs.lock the documentation site (MkDocs) and the screenshot tooling (Playwright) x86_64, Python 3.11

Regenerate with scripts/lock_requirements.sh (uses uv pip compile --generate-hashes). Install with uv pip install --require-hashes -r requirements/<role>.lock or pip install --require-hashes -r .... The edge-server lock pins the x86_64 CPU build of PyTorch (torch==2.1.2+cpu), which is on the PyTorch index: add --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu (and, with uv, --index-strategy unsafe-best-match), or install from the local mirror with --no-index --find-links.

Transformers is pinned to 4.46.3 because the Qwen2 (4.37), Llama 3.2 (4.43) and HeadSplit (4.40) adapters need it; the Chapter 6 experiments of the thesis used 4.36, and the testbed's code accepts both the 4.36 and the 4.38+ interfaces.

The optional INA260 power-monitor packages (power.in) depend on the Raspberry Pi platform (adafruit-blinka) and are installed on the devices only; they are listed without a lock file because their platform wheels cannot be resolved off the device.

docs.title: Results format
docs.text: Every run writes one directory, results/<run id>/, with results/latest pointing at the most recent one. The run id is YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-<6 hex> in UTC. All files are JSON written atomically (a temporary file renamed into place), so a reader never sees a partial file. Synthetic examples of the main files are in ../data/sample/ (labelled as synthetic; regenerate with python -m tests.make_sample_data).

docs.title: The run directory
docs.text:
results/<run id>/
  metadata.json                           scenario, software and hardware facts, written before any device command
  scenario.json                           the scenario version that was run (with defaults filled in)
  journal.json                            every applied change and its undo action, with the outcome of the undo
  summary.json                            status, error, number of teardown failures, main outputs, T0
  logs/merged.log                         time-stamped [node][stream] lines of every remote command
  logs/inference_server.log               the edge-server inference service (when partitioned inference ran)
  raw/<host>_benchmark_<run id>_rep<k>.json   one BenchmarkResults record per device and repetition
  raw/<host>_phases.json                  per-phase timing of the partitioned-inference runs (per device)
  monitor/<host>_monitor.json             ResourceTrace of each device
  power/<host>_power.json                 PowerTrace of each device (when monitoring.power is true)
  latency/<host>_latency.json             latency-and-system record of each device
  load/<host>_load.json                   the load generator's log of applied targets
  verification/<host>_verification.json   the partition-equivalence report of each device (checks.partition_equivalence)
  merged/<node id>__<run id>.json         the device's records and traces aligned on a common origin
  edge_capacity.json                      the edge server's measured FLOP/s on the model
  edge_frequency_state.json               the edge server's previous cpufreq settings (restored at teardown)
  total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json
  calculated_max_partition_points.json  (+ .details.json)
  final_latencies_averages.json
  optimisation/<timestamp>/optimized_partition_scheme.json, scenario.json, search_log.txt
  headsplit/                              HeadSplit runs only: results.json, headsplit_config.yaml, the controller logs
                                          and, with a controller that writes JSON, controller_rep<k>.json

<host> is the device's hostname as transfer_files.sh prefixes it (the node id when hostnames collide, as in local mode).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Intervals are integers in nanoseconds from time.perf_counter_ns(); wall-clock instants are floats in seconds since the epoch (time.time(), NTP-synchronised).
  • Every record carries origin: {wall_time_s, perf_counter_ns} captured together at the start signal. A sample's instant on the wall clock is origin.wall_time_s + (sample.perf_counter_ns - origin.perf_counter_ns) / 1e9; this is how traces of different devices are aligned.
  • Memory in mebibytes, CPU in percent, sizes in bytes, FLOPs as 2 × multiply-accumulates.

docs.title: Measurement records (docs/schemas/benchmark_results.schema.json)
docs.text:
All device-side records share a header: schema_version, kind (benchmark, resource_trace or power_trace), run_id, hostname, node_id, origin, metadata (framework, input shape, baseline resident memory, thread count, the device's FLOP/s).

BenchmarkResults (kind: benchmark): model, repetition, warmup_runs, and

  • stages[]: index (1-based), name, latency_ns, cpu_peak_percent, memory_peak_mb, flops, macs, output_bytes;
  • partition_points[]: for each s in 0..S, cumulative_latency_ns and cumulative_cpu_percent (sums over stages 1..s), cumulative_memory_mb (the largest stage peak among stages 1..s, the memory needed to run them) and transmitted_bytes (the size of the cut tensor; 0 at s = S);
  • phases[] (partitioned-inference runs): s, local_ns, transmission_ns (first byte sent to the server's acknowledgement of the last byte), remote_ns, queue_wait_ns, and the server's wall-clock instants server_arrival_wall_s, server_service_start_wall_s, server_service_end_wall_s.

ResourceTrace (kind: resource_trace): interval_s, nominal_frequency_khz, samples[] with perf_counter_ns, cpu_percent, memory_used_mb, memory_available_mb, temperature_c, frequencies_khz (per core), throttled (the firmware flags).

PowerTrace (kind: power_trace): interval_s, samples[] with perf_counter_ns, current_ma, voltage_v, power_mw.

docs.title: The three thesis output files
docs.text:
total_averages_of_benchmark_results.json (src/benchmarking/result_aggregation.py): per node id, hostname, model, repetitions, run_ids, then stages and partition_points keyed by index with, for every measured quantity, {mean, std, min, max, p95, count} over the repetitions, and the per-phase statistics when partitioned inference ran.

final_latencies_averages.json (src/network/node_statistics.py): per node id, samples, measured_at, average_latency_ms, latency_std_ms, latency_p95_ms, loss_percent (to the edge server), total_memory_mb, available_memory_mb, available_memory_percent, cpu_usage_percent, and targets with the same latency figures per pinged node. The same averages are written into nodes.json as the node's statistics.

calculated_max_partition_points.json (src/benchmarking/partition_calculator.py): {node id: s}, the largest feasible partition point under the memory constraint (cumulative memory up to s within the available memory) and the CPU constraint (baseline usage plus the stage's increment below 100 %). The sibling .details.json lists per node available_memory_mb, baseline_cpu_percent, memory_limited_s, cpu_limited_s, max_partition_point and binding (memory or cpu).

docs.title: Optimisation result
docs.text: optimisation/<timestamp>/optimized_partition_scheme.json (src/partitioning/delay_optimizer.py): optimized_partition_scheme (the vector in device order), by_node, objective, value and value_unit (seconds), algorithm, policy, evaluations, iterations, per_device[] with s, local_ms, transmission_ms, remote_ms, total_ms, the all_local_baseline, the inputs (run id, the scenario's source and SHA-256, the edge capacity, the hashes of the input files) and the path of the search_log.txt, which has one line per evaluated vector. The scenario version is copied next to it.

docs.title: Metadata and journal
docs.text:
metadata.json: schema_version, run_id, created_at, the full scenario, software (the Git commit of the testbed and whether the tree was clean, Python, TensorFlow and PyTorch versions), nodes (per node: hostname, kernel, OS release, CPU model, cores, maximum frequency, memory, NTP status), config (the effective configuration without secrets).

journal.json: entries[] with sequence, node_id, kind (edge_frequency, shaping, load, monitor, cpufreq, cgroup, process, ...), description, undo (the action teardown runs: stop_process, tc_clear, cpufreq_restore, cgroup_remove, edge_freq_restore, stop_local), applied_at, undone, undo_error. A completed run has every entry undone: true with undo_error: null; python -m src.orchestration.experiment teardown undoes the pending entries of unfinished runs.

summary.json: run_id, status (completed or aborted), error, teardown_failures, outputs (edge capacity, optimised vector, ...) and t0.
